_readme: Expectations for the markdown fenced-block half of the `examples` Definition-of-Done gate
(issue #850) — see scripts/markdown-examples-gate.mjs and docs/adr/0022-documentation-example-gate.md.
JSON has no comments, so keys beginning with an underscore are documentation and are ignored.
Every other key is a repository-relative POSIX path. Each entry pins ONE ```logo block by the
SHA-256 fingerprint of its source, so prose edits above a block never churn this file, while
editing the block itself forces a re-triage. That is deliberate: this manifest fingerprints
repository content, so it must be re-derived against the branch it will merge into.
THE RULE: a ```logo block either runs completely clean, or it has an entry here that is
ASSERTED. There is no automatic tolerance. The gate fails when a listed block stops producing
exactly its declared codes/profiles, when it becomes clean (a stale expectation), when a
fingerprint matches no block — or matches two.
kind (and the field it asserts):
prose-fragment          codes     an excerpt; its context lives in the surrounding prose
deliberate-error        codes     the prose teaches this exact diagnostic
not-openlogo            codes     the fence says logo but holds EBNF/word-list text
non-terminating         codes     demonstrates forever / a blocking input, so it hits the budget
profile-not-implemented profiles  needs a profile no implementation provides yet
implementation-behind   codes     the SPEC is right and the runtime has not caught up yet
known-broken            codes     the DOCUMENT is wrong — a real defect, never a mute button
implementation-behind vs known-broken is the distinction to get right. A staged spec-then-code
ruling lands the rule in spec/ before the slice that implements it, so for a while a conforming
program still raises. That block is CORRECT and the runtime is behind; saying `known-broken`
would blame the document. Both require the tracking `issue`, and both entries are DELETED when
the tracked work lands — never re-fingerprinted.
setup (optional): OpenLogo source prepended to the block before it runs, supplying the context
the surrounding prose describes. It lets an excerpt execute to COMPLETION instead of halting on
its first undefined name — which matters because the runtime stops at the first error, so
anything below that line would otherwise be statically checked but never executed. A block with
a setup usually asserts `codes: []`: given this context, it runs clean. `inputs` does the same
for a blocking `input` read, scripting the answer the learner would have typed.
A setup supplies CONTEXT — it is not a fix and not a patch. The gate enforces that: the preamble
must parse, check and execute cleanly ON ITS OWN (so it can neither absorb the block's malformed
structure nor lean on a name the block defines), it must not define a name the block also
defines, and it must not redefine anything OpenLogo provides — any primitive or Heritage surface
spelling, at any nesting depth, in any casing. Keep it faithful to what the prose actually says.
issue (optional on any kind; REQUIRED on known-broken and implementation-behind): the issue
tracking the work. not-openlogo entries carry one too, since a mislabeled fence is also a defect
someone has to fix.
Adding an entry is a triage decision, not a formality: `why` is mandatory and must state only
what is verifiable about the block. If a block is simply wrong, fix the block.

spec/grammar.md.why: The block's own last line is commented `# error: forward is a built-in name`, and the section around it is the normative statement of that rule. Its first five lines are the free half — binding a built-in name — and must stay clean; the `define forward` at the end must raise. Before issue #838 wired `turtlePrimitiveArity` into the declaration-slot rule this block ran CLEAN, so the spec's own worked example silently contradicted the paragraph it illustrates. This entry is what stops that from happening again in either direction: the block now fails if `define forward` becomes legal, and fails if any of the five bindings starts raising.

spec/grammar.md.excerpt: define to end return output op stop throw
spec/grammar.md.why: The keyword inventory: a bare vocabulary listing (it contains `import`/`export`, which is the only reason the profile detector ever read it as a Modules example), not OpenLogo source. The fence language is wrong — ```text would be right — which this gate reports rather than edits, because spec/ is maintainer-owned. Asserted so the listing cannot change unnoticed while mislabeled. `ol-reserved-word` left the observed set with #837: read as source, the listing's `set make local thing` line is a BINDING of the name `make`, and maintainer ruling #833 makes binding any name legal (spec/grammar.md:386). Nothing about the listing changed — only what the checker says about reading it as a program.

spec/tooling.md.why: Layer-1 example: the Finding line under it asserts code=ol-missing-end, stage=parse. Asserting it here keeps the checker's own reference example honest.
Layer-1 example: the Finding line asserts code=ol-bad-token with params={ text: ',' } — commas are not separators in OpenLogo.

Layer-2 example: the Finding line asserts code=ol-unknown-command with a did-you-mean suggestion of `forward`. Listing it turns the diagnostic the prose quotes into an assertion, so the checker's own reference example cannot drift from what the checker actually reports.
Layer-2 example: the Finding line asserts code=ol-not-enough-inputs for `first` with expected=1, actual=0.
Layer-2 example: the Finding line asserts code=ol-not-a-place. `:nums` is undefined here too, because the block is also an excerpt.

Layer-2 example: the Finding line asserts code=ol-no-value — `map` needs the last instruction in its block to make a value. Its `setup` supplies the `:nums` the excerpt reads, so the map body actually runs and the documented diagnostic is asserted against a block that executed rather than one that halted on line 1.
